Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000022

From text 'nicholas1990someobservationson pages 3-5'.

M. G. Nicholas, D. A. Mortimer, L. M. Jones, and R. M. Crispin. Some observations on the wetting and bonding of nitride ceramics. Journal of Materials Science, 25:2679-2689, Jun 1990. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00584866, doi:10.1007/bf00584866. This article has 218 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that aluminum bonds to boron nitride (BN), fabricated and tested after bonding at 1000 °C for 15 minutes, had a measured shear strength of 6.1 ± 2.0 MPa. Among the tested ceramics, BN produced the weakest aluminum bond. The reported failure mode was adhesive/interfacial rather than cohesive: BN specimens failed at the metal–ceramic interface, whereas other specimens fractured at least partly within the ceramic. The excerpt does not provide a separate adhesion-strength value for BN coatings specifically; the 6.1 ± 2.0 MPa value is the measured shear strength of the aluminum–BN joints. It also notes that the joints were well filled and that the metal–ceramic interfaces appeared to be in good contact, despite the relatively low interfacial strength. Therefore, based on this passage, BN bonding fails primarily by adhesive failure at the aluminum–BN interface, not by cohesive fracture through the BN ceramic.


---

## pqac-00000023

From text 'nicholas1990someobservationson pages 1-2'.

M. G. Nicholas, D. A. Mortimer, L. M. Jones, and R. M. Crispin. Some observations on the wetting and bonding of nitride ceramics. Journal of Materials Science, 25:2679-2689, Jun 1990. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00584866, doi:10.1007/bf00584866. This article has 218 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that aluminum-brazed ceramic bonds could reach shear strengths as high as 60 MPa at 1000 °C. However, this value is presented as a general result for the brazed ceramic specimens and is not identified in the supplied pages as specifically applying to aluminum-to-boron-nitride (BN) joints. BN was one of the five ceramics investigated, and aluminum was among the braze materials capable of wetting all five ceramics. The excerpt does not provide a separate adhesion-strength value for BN coatings; indeed, it discusses brazed ceramic-metal joints rather than BN coating adhesion tests. It also does not state whether BN bonding failure was cohesive within the BN or adhesive at the BN/interface boundary. The available text indicates that the study examined wetting, capillarity, microstructure, reactivity, and strength-tested sample configurations, but the supplied pages do not include the relevant BN-specific strength or fractography/failure-mode results. Further pages, especially the results and discussion sections, would be needed to determine the aluminum–BN shear strength, BN coating adhesion strength, and whether failure was cohesive or adhesive.


---

## pqac-00000024

From text 'rudolph2013boronnitriderelease pages 4-7'.

Stephan Rudolph. Boron nitride release coatings. ArXiv, pages 163-170, Sep 2013. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118806364.ch16, doi:10.1002/9781118806364.ch16. This article has 12 citations.

The excerpt does not report a numerical shear strength for aluminum bonds to boron nitride, nor does it provide a quantitative adhesion strength for BN coatings. It only states that boron nitride has poor wettability with molten aluminum, which supports its use as a release agent. Regarding coating adhesion, the text explains that some BN coatings can adhere through particle surface energy alone, provided the specific surface area is at least 25 m²/g, but that most applications require refractory binders to obtain reasonable adherence. Phosphate-containing binders are described as hardening at 800–900°C and producing a strong but brittle bond; alumina- or alumina–silica-based binders are recommended for certain thermal-expansion and temperature conditions, while clay minerals can keep coatings soft. The excerpt does not characterize BN bonding failure as cohesive or adhesive, and it gives no fracture or pull-off test results from which that distinction could be determined.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Material / role | Linear CTE, 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ | Wetting behavior relevant to Al-bearing C63000 | Key reactions / failure significance | Key sources |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Graphite crucible | 2–20, anisotropic | Pure Al interacts weakly with graphite at 1000–1150 °C; wetting increases sharply above ≈1150 °C. After 5 min at 1200 °C, reported contact angle ≈85°; above 1200 °C, spreading and a thin adherent layer occur. These pure-Al results are a conservative mechanistic analogue, not direct Cu–10Al data. | Al in exposed C63000 can react as `4Al + 3C → Al₄C₃`; Al₄C₃ and carbon-bearing interfacial products increase anchoring and carbon/inclusion risk. The ≈1300 °C melt temperature lies in the strongly reactive range demonstrated for pure Al. | CTE: (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000021); wetting and Al₄C₃: (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000013) |
| Hexagonal BN coating | 0.8–7.5, anisotropic | Molten Al contact angle is reported near 160° up to ≈900 °C, then decreases between ≈900 and 1000 °C. Independent experiments found high-temperature wetting and Al–BN bonding by 1000–1150 °C; an Al–BN joint made at 1000 °C for 15 min had shear strength 6.1 ± 2.0 MPa. | BN is normally a non-wetting release layer, but at 1300 °C its protection depends strongly on coating purity, binder chemistry, oxide films, time, and defects. Phosphate binders harden at 800–900 °C into a strong but brittle phase; reaction-assisted wetting can let a skull pull out weak coating or coating–graphite interfaces. | CTE and non-wetting: (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021); high-temperature wetting and bond strength: (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000022); binders: (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024) |
| C63000 solidified skull (Cu–10Al–5Ni–3Fe) | ≈16–18 **[estimate; generic Cu-alloy range]** | No direct Al-on-C63000 wetting angle applies because the skull is the melt itself. The relevant interfaces are C63000/BN or, at defects, C63000/graphite. Its 10 wt% Al supplies substantial chemical activity, but direct Cu–Al/BN and Cu–Al/graphite contact-angle data were not located. | On cooling through roughly 1300 °C to ambient, the skull contracts much more than low-CTE BN and many graphite directions. Differential free contraction is approximately 1–2% **[estimate]**, enough to impose shear/peel stress, especially across thick, brittle, incompletely cured, or locally reacted coating. | Generic CTE/mismatch estimate: (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021); analogous shrinkage-driven ceramic pull-out: (pqac-00000010) |
| Aluminum in the alloy (reactive constituent) | ≈23 **[estimate; solid Al near ambient]** | On BN, Al is strongly non-wetting below ≈900 °C but becomes progressively wetting around 900–1000 °C and above. On graphite, the reported angle falls to ≈85° at 1200 °C after 5 min. An intact Al₂O₃ skin can initially inhibit wetting until it ruptures or is reduced/disrupted. | Al can reduce binder oxides—e.g., `2Al + B₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2B` and `4Al + 3SiO₂ → 2Al₂O₃ + 3Si`—and can form Al₄C₃ on exposed graphite. These reactions can replace a release interface with an adherent Al₂O₃/reaction-product bridge and introduce B or Si into the melt. | Oxide-film effect and BN wetting: (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016); graphite wetting/Al₄C₃: (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000013); CTE estimate and mismatch: (pqac-00000020) |

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Step | Operation | Controlled procedure | Acceptance / **GO** criterion | **NO-GO** condition and action |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm materials and product | Verify crucible is graphite; record BN product, lot, carrier, binder, shelf life, and manufacturer instructions. Obtain written compatibility for graphite, C63000, 1300 °C, argon, and induction service. Treat this procedure as subordinate to the atomizer and coating manufacturers’ instructions. | Materials and approved data sheet are identified and traceable. | Unknown crucible, binder, or nozzle material: stop and obtain confirmation before coating. |
| 2 | Select coating chemistry | Prefer high-purity hBN with the least reactive binder available and explicit approval for graphite and Al-bearing copper at 1300 °C. An alumina-based refractory binder is the preferred starting class for >1000 °C; avoid silica/silicate or B₂O₃-rich products where composition purity matters. Phosphate binders harden at 800–900 °C into strong but brittle bonds and are identified for low-expansion ceramics—not high-expansion metal substrates—so use on graphite only with explicit vendor approval (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000024). | Vendor approves product, cure, and chemistry; binder composition is disclosed sufficiently to assess Al, B, Si, and P contamination. | Generic BN aerosol or unknown proprietary binder: do not use for the production run; first qualify it on a graphite coupon with a C63000 melt test. |
| 3 | Protect critical features | Remove the hBN nozzle and BN stopper if permitted; otherwise mask the nozzle seat, thermocouple features, sealing faces, threads, and gas passages. Never spray through or into the ≈0.5 mm bore. | All functional surfaces and passages are positively protected and later inspectable. | Any coating, loose powder, or masking residue enters the bore or sealing interface: clean and borescope/gauge it before proceeding. |
| 4 | Remove residual metal | Warm only enough to release the skull **[estimate: 80–150 °C]**. Lift it without levering against the coating. Remove residual metal with wood, polymer, or another softer nonmetallic tool; do not use steel scrapers or impacts. | No visible metal remains; graphite is not gouged or cracked. | Bonded metal requires force or flexing of the crucible: stop; strip locally under magnification rather than prying. |
| 5 | Decide patch versus full strip | Because the Run-A coating detached in crescents and Run B exposed those areas, fully strip the melt-contact zone to a stable boundary; a complete strip and recoat is preferred for this next diagnostic run. Patch only an isolated defect smaller than about 5 mm with firmly adherent surrounding coating **[estimate]** and only if the same qualified product is used. | Uniform, sound substrate or uniformly adherent retained coat; no feathered, lifted edges. | Multiple bare spots, cracking, blistering, metal undercutting, mixed products, or uncertain cure history: strip the entire melt-contact surface. |
| 6 | Dry-strip loose coating | Vacuum loose material using a HEPA system. Lightly hand-abrade only where needed with clean 320–600 grit SiC paper or a dedicated fine abrasive pad **[estimate]**; use minimal pressure and preserve crucible dimensions. Do not grit-blast unless the crucible vendor authorizes it. | Surface is uniformly matte and free of loose flakes, polished metal smears, and sharp coating steps. | Deep scratches, exposed porosity, dimensional change at the bottom/nozzle seat, or cracks: reject or obtain vendor disposition. |
| 7 | Clean without introducing water | Vacuum again, then wipe with lint-free cloth lightly wetted with reagent-grade IPA or acetone, subject to site safety rules. Use fresh cloths until no grey/metallic residue transfers. Do not soak porous graphite, rinse it with water, use chlorinated cleaner, or touch it with bare hands. Water-based BN systems require forced drying; alcohol carriers reduce the initial water load (pqac-00000000). | Final cloth is clean; solvent has fully evaporated; no oil, fingerprints, dust, or odor remains. | Persistent contamination or absorbed solvent: repeat cleaning and warm-dry; do not coat a damp or oily crucible. |
| 8 | Pre-dry bare crucible | Bake before coating under flowing dry argon or vacuum: ramp 1–3 °C/min to 120 °C, hold 1–2 h, then to 200–250 °C and hold 1–2 h **[estimate]**. Cool under dry inert gas to the coating manufacturer’s application temperature. Avoid prolonged air heating because graphite oxidizes increasingly above about 400 °C (pqac-00000001). | No condensate or pressure/outgassing anomaly; mass on a witness coupon is stable **[estimate: <0.1% change over the final hour]**. | Continued outgassing, odor, condensate, or mass loss: extend the hold and investigate contamination. |
| 9 | Prepare coating | Mechanically mix or roll until completely homogeneous; do not entrain foam. Filter only through the mesh specified by the vendor. Adjust viscosity solely with the specified carrier. Prepare a graphite witness coupon alongside the crucible. | No settled agglomerates, skin, gel, or expired material; spray pattern is uniform on a test card. | Lumps, irreversible settling, contamination, or unauthorized dilution: discard the batch. |
| 10 | Apply first coat | Spray rather than brush for uniformity. Rudolph reports a 1.5 mm spray-gun nozzle as suitable (pqac-00000000). Apply a light mist/tie coat to a warm substrate **[estimate: 40–80 °C]**, rotating the crucible to avoid pools. Keep coating out of the bore and sealing surfaces. | Continuous thin grey-white veil with no runs, pinholes caused by oil, or powder piles. | Runs, mud cracking, fish-eyes, or blocked features: remove the defective wet coat, reclean, and restart. |
| 11 | Flash-dry between coats | Dry each coat at ambient for 10–20 min, then at 80–120 °C for 30–60 min **[estimates; use product data sheet if different]**. Water-based coatings require forced drying (pqac-00000000). Allow the layer to dry before recoating. | Coat is uniformly matte, non-tacky, and does not mark under a gentle gloved touch on a noncritical rim or witness coupon. | Cool/dark damp areas, bubbling, tackiness, or solvent odor: extend drying; do not trap carrier beneath another coat. |
| 12 | Build final coating | Apply 2–4 light coats **[estimate]**, cross-coating successive passes. Target total dry thickness 50–150 µm **[estimate; initial qualification target: 75–100 µm]**. Keep local variation within approximately ±25 µm **[estimate]**. Thin layers are preferred; overly thick brittle coatings store more mismatch stress. Very thin BN layers can provide release behavior, and foundry applications may be recoated between casts (pqac-00000002). | Uniform coverage without runs, exposed graphite, thick ridges, or measurable intrusion into fits; witness-coupon thickness is within target. | Less than 50 µm, more than 150 µm, or local accumulations: correct before final cure; if already dry and cracked, strip and restart. |
| 13 | Low-temperature dry | After the final coat, air-dry ≥2 h **[estimate]**, then heat in dry argon or vacuum at 1–2 °C/min to 120 °C and hold 2 h; continue to 250 °C and hold 1–2 h **[estimate]**. Vent water/solvent safely. | No bubbling, blistering, flaking, or sustained outgassing; coating remains uniform. | Any blister or delamination: stop, cool, strip the affected system, and correct surface preparation or coat thickness. |
| 14 | Binder cure | Follow the product-specific cure exactly. If an inorganic coating requires a high-temperature cure, use dry argon or qualified vacuum—not air—above the graphite oxidation range. **Provisional qualification schedule [estimate]:** ramp 1–3 °C/min to 400 °C, hold 1 h; then to 800–900 °C, hold 1 h; cool at ≤3 °C/min under inert gas. Phosphate systems harden at 800–900 °C and become strong but brittle (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000012). Do not take an organic-bound aerosol directly into a production melt without its specified burnout cycle. | Witness coupon and crucible show no smoke, odor, bubbles, cracks, or powder shedding; furnace oxygen and exhaust remain within approved limits. | No approved cure schedule, persistent off-gassing, rapid temperature excursion, air leak, or coating damage: no production melt. |
| 15 | Optional service-temperature qualification | Before first production use, qualify the selected coating on a graphite witness coupon—or a sacrificial crucible—through the intended 1300 °C argon cycle. BN’s behavior with Al changes markedly above 900–1000 °C, and Al–BN joints made at 1000 °C for 15 min reached 6.1 ± 2.0 MPa shear strength, so low-temperature appearance alone does not establish release at 1300 °C (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022). | Coupon survives without reaction glazing, spallation, or strong C63000 adhesion; chemistry remains acceptable. | Glazed/wetted areas, strong metal attachment, binder reaction, or flakes: reject that product/schedule and consult the supplier. |
| 16 | Inspect coverage | Under bright oblique light and 5–10× magnification **[estimate]**, inspect 100% of the bottom, wall, transition radii, nozzle seat, and stopper-contact area. Photograph and map the surface. Use UV tracer only if supplied/approved. | No bare graphite, pinholes, cracks, blisters, loose powder, ridges, foreign matter, or coating in excluded areas. | Any defect in the melt-contact zone or near the nozzle: no-go until stripped/repaired and recured. |
| 17 | Check adhesion and thickness | Measure the witness coupon by mass/area or cross-section; use a calibrated eddy-current/ultrasonic method only if validated for BN on graphite. Perform a gentle dry lint-free wipe on the witness and a low-tack tape test only if the coating supplier permits it. Do not score the production crucible. | No flake transfer; only slight pigment transfer if the product is intentionally soft; thickness is within the qualified range. | Flakes, exposed graphite, cohesive chunks, or failed witness adhesion: reject and recoat. |
| 18 | Inspect nozzle and stopper | Clean and inspect the hBN nozzle and BN stopper separately. Pass the manufacturer’s bore gauge or optical measurement through the ≈0.5 mm bore; inspect alignment, chips, deposits, and the sealing line. Apply BN coating to these parts only if their manufacturer specifies it; solid hBN generally should not receive an uncontrolled thick paint layer. | Bore is dimensionally correct and unobstructed; stopper seats uniformly; no loose particles. | Any uncertain bore, crack, chipped edge, coating lump, or poor seal: replace the component. |
| 19 | Final moisture-removal bake | Within 24 h of charging **[estimate]**, rebake assembled compatible parts under dry argon or vacuum: 1–2 °C/min to 150–200 °C, hold 1–2 h **[estimate]**, then keep sealed under dry argon. If storage exceeds 24–48 h or humidity exposure occurs, repeat. | No condensate or abnormal outgassing; system remains dry and protected until charging. | Humidity exposure, cold storage condensation, or unexplained pressure rise: repeat bake and leak check. |
| 20 | Pre-run **GO / NO-GO** release | Record coating product/lot, dry thickness, cure trace, witness result, crucible photos, nozzle bore, stopper seating, argon dew point/O₂, pressure reference (gauge versus absolute), and planned end-of-pour sequence. Reinspect after installation. | **GO only if every preceding criterion passes, the manufacturer approves the coating/cure for graphite and 1300 °C C63000, and the nozzle/stopper are clean and aligned.** | **NO-GO** for any bare graphite, loose coating, unknown binder/cure, dampness, blocked or uncertain bore, damaged hBN, graphite crack, failed witness coupon, or unqualified patch. |
| 21 | Post-run maintenance | Photograph before skull removal. Drain completely while hot using the validated pressure sequence; after cooling, remove residual metal without levering. Inspect and map damage after every melt. Rudolph reports recoating foundry surfaces between casting cycles, though the exact interval must be qualified for this system (pqac-00000002). | Retain only a fully adherent, defect-free coating within its qualified melt count; record trend data. | Any crescent pull-out, exposed graphite, cracking, contamination, or nozzle debris: retire the coating and fully recoat rather than repeatedly patching it. |

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title

        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?

Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: a charge is induction-melted in a crucible,
argon over-pressure ("graining" pressure) pushes the melt through a bottom nozzle once a stopper
(sealing) rod is lifted, the stream falls onto an inclined plate driven by an ultrasonic sonotrode
(booster plus horn), and melt that the plate does not atomize runs off into a catch crucible below.
A separate "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar to push the melt out (it replaces, rather than adds to, the
graining pressure). Pressures are read on the HMI; whether they are gauge or absolute is unconfirmed.

Alloy: nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 ("630 bronze" rod; Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; liquidus ~1054 C;
liquid density ~6.9-7.0 g/cm3; surface tension ~1.1-1.3 N/m). Melt setpoint 1300 C (the module's
hard limit; ~245 C superheat), read by a thermocouple at the crucible. Crucible: graphite (material to
be confirmed) with its interior sprayed with a boron nitride paint; BN stopper rod; hBN nozzle (bore
about 0.5 mm, to be confirmed). Plate: carbon-fiber composite coated with tungsten (the vendor's
W-coated plate for copper alloys). Booster 1:1.5. Argon atmosphere. In training with aluminum, the
vendor's trainer set the plate so that the melt landed on the plate and rolled down about a third of
the plate's length before it atomized.

Run A (27 Oct): new plate, fresh BN coat, new nozzle, 1080 g charge (four rod pieces), O2 24 ppm,
amplitude 90%, graining 0.19 bar, held 2 min after the charge melted. The stream hit right at the
lower (free) end of the plate. The melt kept flowing only while the operator held the turbo (1.5 bar)
for most of the run; ~97% of the charge was collected as powder, with a visible fraction of flakes.
A thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling, BN came away with
it: light grey crescents of BN on the underside of the skull match the bare patches in the crucible's
coat.

Run B (28 Oct): the same plate (second use; it looked fine), the same nozzle (the bore looked clear),
the same crucible with small bare patches where the BN had come off (not recoated), 858 g charge (five
rod pieces), O2 11 ppm, amplitude 90% for the first quarter of the pour, then 100%; graining 0.23 bar
at the start, back to 0.19 bar about halfway; held 1 min after melting. The plate was moved up a little
so that the stream landed farther up the plate rather than at its very end. Result: the melt "really
struggled to atomize"; some powder was made, but most of the charge ended up as a solid puck in the
catch crucible. Changing amplitude and pressure during the pour did not help.

Focus on the boron nitride coating of the crucible (and of the stopper rod and nozzle). Give numbers
with sources (manufacturer data sheets, foundry practice, papers with DOIs) and mark any estimate.

1. Why would a C63000 skull bond to a sprayed BN coat strongly enough to pull the coat off the
   crucible on cooling? Consider the binders in common BN paints and aerosols (aluminum phosphate,
   silicate, B2O3, organic binders), reaction of the Al in the melt with B2O3 or silica in the binder
   (and the wetting this causes), Al2O3 films, thermal contraction mismatch, coat thickness, and
   whether the coat was fully dried and baked before the first melt.
2. Best practice for re-applying BN on a graphite crucible used for copper alloys and aluminum
   bronze: surface preparation (removing loose coating and skull residue; abrading or not; solvent
   cleaning; avoiding water), stripping the whole coat versus patching the bare spots, number of coats,
   target thickness, drying time between coats, the cure or bake schedule (temperature, atmosphere such
   as air, argon or vacuum, and ramp rate), re-baking to drive off absorbed moisture before use, how to
   check coverage and adhesion, and how many melts a coat typically lasts. Include vendor guidance
   with numbers (for example ZYP Coatings BN Lubricoat and Hardcoat, Momentive or Saint-Gobain Combat
   BN paints, Henze BN, 3M) and say which product types suit an aluminum-containing copper melt.
3. What a patched or partly bare coat does to a C63000 melt at 1300 C: wetting of bare graphite by
   Cu-Al melts (Al4C3 formation), carbon pickup, skull adhesion and melt retention, flakes of coating,
   binder or skull entering the melt and lodging in a ~0.5 mm nozzle bore or otherwise disturbing the
   stream, and B, Si or P pickup in the powder. Could the bare patches or coating debris plausibly
   have caused run B's poor atomization, or are they mainly a contamination and crucible-life issue?
4. Avoiding and removing the skull: draining the crucible fully, end-of-pour pressure, crucible shape,
   keeping the crucible hot until drained, and removing a skull without taking the coat with it.
5. Alternatives for aluminum bronze: thicker or hard-coat BN, solid hBN or pyrolytic BN liners,
   alumina, zirconia or magnesia crucibles, and zirconia or yttria washes.
6. A step-by-step recoat, cure and inspection procedure for the next run, with a go/no-go checklist.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Graphene nanoplatelet (GNP)-reinforced metal matrix composites (MMCs) represent a groundbreaking group of lightweight structural materials, offering exceptional combinations of strength, toughness, and multifunctionality that are critical for next-generation applications.                     <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    bubbling in magnesium alloys to form carbon–metal (C–M) bonds. Particular emphasis is placed on mechanisms of C–M bonding, dispersion challenges, and interfacial bonding between the metallic matrices and graphene. This review emphasizes the potential of graphene-reinforced MMCs across industries and identifies the persistent barriers to process upscaling.

Abstract:
<jats:p><p>Magnesium is a lightweight metal with a high strength-to-weight ratio, making it an ideal material for improving fuel efficiency. However, its poor mechanical properties necessitate the need for researchers to find ways of improving them for this material to find wider acceptance in industry. This study examines the grain refinement capabilities of an aluminum-carbon (graphite) composite in cast AZ91E magnesium alloy. With increasing carbon addition, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and ductility improved, while yield strength (YS) remained largely unchanged. The fracture mechanism also remained unchanged with increasing carbon addition, showing mixed-mode fracture in samples of highest and lowest ductility. The nucleation mechanism was determined to be duplex nucleation of Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub> and Al<sub>8</sub>Mn<sub>5</sub>. X-ray diffraction analysis confirmed that the Al-C inoculant contained Al4C3 after sintering; however, most Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub> was formed in-situ during the melting and casting process.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p> The annual generation of industrial solid waste has exceeded 10 billion metric tons, and its resource recovery poses a major challenge to global sustainable development. This paper reviews research progress on the preparation of ceramic-metal composites using typical industrial wastes—such as red mud, fly ash, coal gangue, zinc furnace slag, waste refractory materials, recycled aluminum, and aluminum ash—as raw materials through processes including high-temperature sintering, carbon thermal reduction, and hot-press forging. It reveals common patterns across different waste-to-material conversion pathways: (1) “harmful components” in the waste can be redefined as “functional components”; (2) the low-melting-point aluminosilicate liquid phase plays a dual role as both a reaction medium and an interfacial binder in all high-temperature systems, and its viscosity-temperature relationship directly determines the pore structure and interfacial bonding strength; (3) Dispersion strengthening and grain boundary pinning of the reinforcing phase are universal mechanisms for enhancing hardness and strength; however, an increase in the ceramic phase is typically accompanied by a decrease in elongation. Nevertheless, all systems face common bottlenecks: energy consumption at each stage has not been quantitatively assessed over the entire life cycle; there is a lack of systematic research on how fluctuations in raw material composition affect product consistency; and a scale-up pathway from batch laboratory operations to continuous industrial production has yet to be established.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Black phosphorus is one of the emerging members of two-dimensional (2D) materials which has recently entered the biomedical field. Its anisotropic properties and infrared bandgap have enabled researchers to discover its applicability in several fields including optoelectronics, 3D printing, bioimaging, and others. Characterization techniques such as Raman spectroscopy have revealed the structural information of Black phosphorus (BP) along with its fundamental properties, such as the behavior of its photons and electrons. The present review provides an overview of synthetic approaches and properties of BP, in addition to a detailed discussion about various types of surface modifications available for overcoming the stability-related drawbacks and for imparting targeting ability to synthesized nanoplatforms. The review further gives an overview of multiple characterization techniques such as spectroscopic, thermal, optical, and electron microscopic techniques for providing an insight into its fundamental properties. These characterization techniques are not only important for the analysis of the synthesized BP but also play a vital role in assessing the doping as well as the structural integrity of BP-based nanocomposites. The potential role of BP and BP-based nanocomposites for biomedical applications specifically, in the fields of drug delivery, 3D printing, and wound dressing, have been discussed in detail to provide an insight into the multifunctional role of BP-based nanoplatforms for the management of various diseases, including cancer therapy. The review further sheds light on the role of BP-based 2D platforms such as BP nanosheets along with BP-based 0D platforms—i.e., BP quantum dots in the field of therapy and bioimaging of cancer using techniques such as photoacoustic imaging and fluorescence imaging. Although the review inculcates the multimodal therapeutic as well as imaging role of BP, there is still research going on in this field which will help in the development of BP-based theranostic platforms not only for cancer therapy, but various other diseases.

Abstract:
In this review, we analyze the structure of multicomponent alloys without principal components (they are also called high entropy alloys—HEAs), containing not only metals but also hydrogen, nitrogen, carbon, boron, or silicon. In particular, we discuss the phenomenon of grain boundary (GB) wetting by the melt or solid phase. The GB wetting can be complete or incomplete (partial). In the former case, the grains of the matrix are completely separated by the continuous layer of the second phase (solid or liquid). In the latter case of partial GB wetting, the second solid phase forms, between the matrix grains, a chain of (usually lenticular) precipitates or droplets with a non-zero value of the contact angle. To deal with the morphology of GBs, the new GB tie-lines are used, which can be constructed in the two- or multiphase areas of the multidimensional HEAs phase diagrams. The GBs in HEAs in the case of complete or partial wetting can also contain hydrides, nitrides, carbides, borides, or silicides. Thus, GB wetting by the hydrides, nitrides, carbides, borides, or silicides can be used in the so-called grain boundary chemical engineering in order to improve the properties of respective HEAs.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal foams offer attractive properties for lightweight structures. This study presents the development of a powder metallurgical aluminum alloy intended for foamable wires that can be used in additive manufacturing processes such as wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Unlike established aluminum wrought alloys, whose melting range is not well suited for foaming, or cast alloys which are not easily extruded into thin wires, the custom AlMg2Si1.2 alloy developed in this study combines a melting interval matched to the decomposition of pre-oxidized blowing agent (TiH
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) with a low alloying content suitable for high extrusion ratios. For this, the alloy composition was determined using thermodynamic calculations. The material was then cast into billets, which were extruded into rod electrodes. Pre-alloyed metal powder was produced from these electrodes using electrode induction melting inert gas atomization (EIGA), and the influence of atomization gas parameters on powder properties was investigated. Increasing the gas pressure from 16.8 bar to 23.0 bar reduced the median particle size from 51 to 40 µm. The best flowability was observed for the fraction 63–90 µm. A solidus temperature of 560 °C and a liquidus of 646 °C were determined by differential scanning calorimetry, aligning with the principal hydrogen-release peak of the blowing agent. Foam samples produced from the powder confirmed the material’s foamability, reaching porosities of 64–68%, as determined by X-ray microscopy. These results indicate that AlMg2Si1.2 processed via EIGA yields reproducible, highly porous foams, and is a suitable basis for foamable wires in WAAM.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The quality of the feedstock powder plays a key role in determining the properties of coatings produced by cold spray (CS). However, most commercially available powders are not specifically designed for CS, which makes it difficult to tailor powder characteristics for optimal performance. In this study, we examined the cold sprayability of five copper (Cu) powders manufactured using electrolysis, gas atomization, and mechanical grinding. The powders were characterized in terms of their microstructure, particle shape, and size distribution to evaluate how the production method influences powder properties. Powder flowability was measured using a shear cell test, while mechanical properties and deformability relevant to CS were assessed through nano-indentation. The results showed that gas-atomized powders with equiaxed grain structures offered the best combination of flowability and deformability, making them the most suitable for CS. Their spherical particle shape resulted in a lower surface area compared to the irregular electrolytic powder, which reduced inter-particle surface forces and allowed for smoother powder flow. Nano-indentation measurements indicated that the mechanically ground powder with ultra-fine grains and the gas-atomized powder containing fine dendrites had the highest nano-hardness values (HIT = 2.1 ± 0.15 GPa and 1.6 ± 0.1 GPa, respectively). In contrast, the porous electrolytic Cu powder showed the lowest hardness (HIT = 0.7 ± 0.2 GPa). These trends were confirmed by microstructural analysis of the deposited coatings. Coatings produced from the irregular electrolytic powder exhibited limited particle deformation, weak inter-particle bonding, and the highest porosity. Conversely, spherical gas-atomized powders produced much denser coatings. In particular, the powder with the most uniform spherical shape and no microsatellite particles resulted in the lowest coating porosity due to its superior deformation behavior upon impact.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cold spray deposition was investigated as a candidate technology for producing corrosion- and abrasion-resistant coatings for deep borehole nuclear waste disposal canisters. Commercially pure grade 2 Ti, Cu, Cu-1 wt.% alumina and Inconel 625 were deposited on AISI C1020 steel with thicknesses between 0.9 and 3.2 mm. Coating adhesion to steel was generally poor under nitrogen propellant but improved when the initial layer was deposited using helium. All coatings exhibited residual porosity. Post-spray heat treatments were applied to reduce open porosity: laser glazing for Ti and Inconel 625 and furnace heat treatment (350 °C, 1 h in air) for the Cu-based coatings. Laser treatment significantly refined the microstructure and reduced open porosity in the Ti coatings. Electrochemical testing in 0.1 M NaCl confirmed that corrosion resistance increased markedly with coating thickness and was substantially higher for Ti and Inconel 625 than for the Cu-based coatings. Furnace heat treatment enhanced corrosion resistance by approximately one order of magnitude, whereas laser glazing improved performance by roughly two orders of magnitude. Abrasion resistance (ASTM G65-00) decreased in the order: Inconel 625 >  > Cu + alumina ≈ Cu > CP2-Ti. Laser glazing improved the abrasion resistance of Ti by ~ 70%, surpassing Cu + alumina, whereas heat treatments had minimal influence on the other materials. Microhardness increased significantly after cold spray due to severe plastic deformation and was partially restored toward feedstock values after heat exposure for Cu-based and Inconel 625 coatings. Laser glazing nearly doubled the hardness of Ti owing to surface TiN formation. These results emphasize the critical role of eliminating open porosity to achieve high corrosion resistance in cold-sprayed coatings, while also identifying strategies for improving abrasion resistance in coatings intended for deep borehole disposal applications.</jats:p>

Lubrication properties

Due to the layer structure mentioned before both boron nitride and graphite can be used as high
temperature solid lubricants. However, the lubrication property strongly depends upon the
temperature range of intended application. Figure 5 shows the coefficient of friction for boron

                                          166nitride compared with that of graphite in the temperature range from 20  ... 1000°C (5). At
temperatures up to 600°C graphite shows a lower coefficient of friction than boron nitride. The
strong increase of values between 600 and 800°C is caused by the oxidation of graphite. Here,
boron nitride shows advantageous values of the coefficient of friction. The climb in the curve of
boron nitride between 800  ... 1000°C is caused by its oxidation and subsequently forming of

Wetting behaviour

One of the most well-known properties of boron nitride is its poor wettability against many
metal melts. These include among others melts of aluminium and magnesium. The wetting of
ceramic material by a melt is usually described by the wetting angle 0 which is determined by
using a heating microscope according to the method of the sessile drop. Here, the contact angle
0 of a melt drop is measured on the substrate (see Figure 6). Large angles (>90°) mean a poor
wettability according to the drawn example, small angles (<90°C) in contrasts represent a good
 wettability.

          describe their wetting behaviour.



                                          167Figure 7 shows the contact angles of molten aluminium in contact with boron nitride, silicon
nitride and alumina in dependence of the temperature (6). Up to 900°C boron nitride is only
poorly wetted by aluminium and shows contact angles of 160°C. Between 900  ... 1000°C the
contact angle value decreases, but is well above those of A^Os and SisN^ However, in the
temperature range which is interesting to aluminium casters, the wetting behaviour of boron
nitride is far superior to oxide ceramics like alumina and even a little better than other nitrides
like silicon nitride. Thus boron nitride  is an ideal release agent  for casting and shaping
processes in light metal casthouses and foundries.

Composition of coatings based on boron nitride

Various types of boron nitride coatings are available on the market. They differ in types of
boron nitride used for the production of such coatings, in carrier liquids preferred as well as in
the solid content and refractory binder.

Boron nitride

Boron nitride are commercially available with BN concentrations between 95 and 98 mass-%
 for refractory and common casting applications. If higher BN concentrations are required, e. g.
 for laboratory and research applications, BN concentrations >98.5 mass-%. The balance will be
 mainl

 Carrier liquids

 The choice of carrier liquids is mainly governed by technological aspects, but other points of
 view such as environmental and safety concerns must also taken into account. Water is an
 inexpensive, readily available and non-hazardous option. However, forced drying of applied
 coatings will be necessary in most cases. Alternatively organic solvents such as alcohols
 (ethanol, 2-propanol) may be used, but these formulations have to be labelled according to
 hazardous materials regulations.

                                          168Refractory binder

Boron nitride coatings can be produced without any refractory binder; the adherence of the
particles can be achieved with their surface energy alone. Specific surface areas of at least
25m2/g are necessary for this. Most applications, however, require a coating with reasonable
adherence which makes the use of refractory binders necessary. For coating ceramic substrates
with low thermal expansion, phosphate-containing binders have proven to be well suited. These
binders harden when heated to 800 ... 900°C and result in a strong yet brittle bond. They cannot
be used for high-thermal-expansion substrates like metals. Here binders on the basis of A^Os
for higher temperatures (>1000°C) or AkOs-SiC^ for temperatures below 1000°C can be used.
If the coating is meant to remain soft throughout the whole temperature range, clay minerals
may be the binder of choice.

Application of coatings based on boron nitride

In order to use boron nitride in casthouses and foundries it is necessary to apply in the form of
coatings. In most cases these coatings are water-based suspensions like house paint. These
boron-nitride-coatings are applied like ordinary house paints by brushing or dipping. If  it is
required to coat small objects, dipping can be an application method of choice as well. Spraying
is also possible and is recommended for coating larger surfaces and for hot objects which are
difficult to paint. For spraying, a blow cup or a spray gun operated by pressurized air can be
used. Nozzle sizes of 1.5mm will give best results.

Application to DC casting systems

The most commonly used application of Boron-Nitride-Coating in the DC casting process is the
coating of mould transition plates. A coat of boron-nitride-coating ensures the non-wetting of
the melt during casting and the release of remains of aluminium during the casting breaks,
boron-nitride-coating  is applied to the ceramic  transition plate by brushing or  spraying.
However, with the application it is important not to coat the porous graphite ring, because this
would interrupt the gas flow through the mould.

Another similar application of boron-nitride-coating is the coating of the thimbles, usually
made of fused  silica, boron-nitride-coating is applied by brushing or spraying on the inner
surface. This enables the operator to easily remove the remaining metal during the casting
breaks. The coating is applied before the casting table is put into service for the first time and
between casting breaks when the remaining metal is removed.

The third application to DC machines is the coating of the refractory lining of the distribution
trough. In contrast to the application to transition plates and thimbles discussed before, this
application is done by spraying. However, the first coat can be done by brushing. The spraying
is done during each casting break, when the trough is tilted and the casting pit emptied. The
boron nitride ensures an easy and quick removal of the remaining aluminium. The boron-
nitride-coating makes cleaning of the trough easier and is well accepted by the working force.

## 2. rudolph2013boronnitriderelease pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000001)

          BORON NITRIDE RELEASE COATINGS

                             Stephan Rudolph
                    Euro fur angewandte Mineraloge
                              Tonisvorst, Germany

                                      Abstract

Boron  nitride  is an advanced  ceramic  material with outstanding chemical and thermal
properties. It is often called "white graphite" because  it has a graphite-like structure, but in
contrast to graphite, it is white. It is an excellent high-temperature solid lubricant, is stable at
high temperature and - most important for casting and foundry applications - is not wetted by
many metallic melts like aluminium, magnesium and zinc.

In order to be able to use the advantages of boron nitride in casthouse and foundry applications,
we developed coatings on the basis of boron nitride particularly for the application within
casting shops. These coatings are applied like ordinary house paints by brushing or using a
spray gun. They are perfect release agents used in aluminium foundries for the protection of
ladles,  dies ingot mould, permanent moulds thermocouples and ceramic  structures. These
coatings provide an excellent non- sticking and lubricating surface to which neither aluminium
nor magnesium will adhere.

Boron nitride coatings are also proven release agents for coating thimbles, transition plates and
refractory linings of distribution troughs of DC casting machines. During casting breaks, these
coatings ensure the perfect and easy release of remaining aluminium without damaging the
refractory substrate.

Boron nitride release coatings are available as water-based paints as concentrates as well as
ready-to-use formulations. For an easier application in suitable environments, these coatings are
available in aerosol cans too.

In contrast to graphite coatings and other (red mud) readily-used coatings boron nitride release
coatings are stable in air (up to 1000°C), show excellent non-wetting behaviour (the best in the
field of ceramics) and very good lubrication properties even at high temperatures. These very
advanced characteristics make boron nitride release coatings a product of the first choice to
foundrymen.





                                                    7th Australian Asian Pacific Conference
                                   Aluminium Cast House Technology
                                               Edited by P.R. Whiteley
                       IMS (The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society), 2001


                                          163Introduction

Release coatings are used in DC casting, ingot casting, sand casting and with different die
casting processes. Beyond that they are used as a surface protection for ladles, troughs, launders
and various other equipment which come into contact with metallic melts. They have the
function

- to prevent a reaction of the melt with the mould material,
- to influence the heat transfer locally between melt and shaping surface,
- to enable a separation between casting and the mould when discharging the mould.

Beyond that coatings may react neither with the melt nor with the mould material. The coating
should be able to be applied with an even layer thickness on the shaping surfaces, should not
adhere at the surface of the cast parts partially and, if they are applied on as wear-coating, they
should not build up.

Beyond that release coatings should be environmentally  friendly. The characteristics  like
chemical and thermal stability, thermal conductivity and separation efficiency, necessary for
the  fulfilment  of these  functions, depend primarily on the  refractory  fillers used  in the
respective coatings.

Beside the classical refractory fillers such as graphite, zircon or talc also the use of advanced
ceramic materials  is considered. Here above  all boron nitride  is to be mentioned, which
indicates a number of interesting characteristics, which make the use as a refractory  filler in
release coatings to appear meaningful (1,2).

Physical and chemical characteristics of boron nitride and comparison with graphite

Boron nitride occurs in two modifications. The cubic high pressure modification however is
ignored in the following paper and only the hexagonal modification is regarded. In the literature
the hexagonal boron nitride is often called "white graphite", since  it shows a structure very
similar  to  that  of  graphite.  Therefore   it  appears meaningful  to  compare  the  physical
characteristics of boron nitride with those of graphite. Some important physical characteristics
are shown in Table I.

                                          164 Crystal structure

 Both boron nitride and graphite crystallize in a hexagonal layer lattice with a very similar layer
 distance (see Figure 1) (3,  4). While for boron nitride a layer distance of 666.1pm was
 measured, graphite shows a value of 669,6pm. Additionally both materials show similar
 densities and Mohs hardness. Rubbed between fingers both substances appear similar to talc.
 This is due to the plate-like formation of both materials. The layers of the lattice may be shifted
 easily, therefore both graphite as well as boron nitride are suitable as solid lubricants. A
 scanning electron micrograph (Figure 2) shows the plate-like particles of boron nitride powder
used as a starting material for boron nitride coatings

Thermal stability

However large differences can be observed to thermal stability and oxidation resistance of
boron nitride and graphite. Both materials show a very high point of sublimation which is
clearly situated above that of other ceramic materials. In Figure 3 the melting points or points
                                         165of sublimation of  different  ceramic materials  are shown. Thus graphite has a point  of
sublimation of 3650°C. Boron nitride with a sublimation point of almost 3000°C is in second
place. This is clearly above other ceramic materials such as SisN^ SiC or A^Os or even ZrOi.
However,  the  application  temperature  of  all  ceramic  materials  is  well  below  these
melting/sublimation points.

Under reducing conditions boron nitride can be used to about 1650°C, graphite in contrast to

breaks. The coating is applied before the casting table is put into service for the first time and
between casting breaks when the remaining metal is removed.

The third application to DC machines is the coating of the refractory lining of the distribution
trough. In contrast to the application to transition plates and thimbles discussed before, this
application is done by spraying. However, the first coat can be done by brushing. The spraying
is done during each casting break, when the trough is tilted and the casting pit emptied. The
boron nitride ensures an easy and quick removal of the remaining aluminium. The boron-
nitride-coating makes cleaning of the trough easier and is well accepted by the working force.
The recoat is done after each casting. However, in contrast to terracote red mud coatings and
bone ash coatings, extremely thin layers for this coating are needed only for a successful
application.

Casting of ingots

Boron-nitride-coatings find  its application in the area of the secondary metal producers and
recycling firms, too. With this application the ingot moulds are coated in order to ensure for the
                                          169perfect release and high quality surfaces of their ingots. The boron-nitride-coatings can be used
for casting aluminium and magnesium as well as for zinc and lead. When casting magnesium
with boron-nitride-coatings it will be noticed that the formation of oxides of the surface of the
ingots is suppressed. This makes recycling of magnesium easier because the oxides cannot be
removed from the melt because of their density being in the same order of magnitude of the
molten metal.

Die casting / gravity die casting

It is generally known to use boron-nitride-coatings for the coating of dies in gravity die casting
and low pressure die casting processes. The very good high temperature lubricating and release
properties ensure the perfect release of the casting from the mould. The boron-nitride-coating
dramatically reduces the sticking of the casting to the mould. The boron-nitride-coating also
suppresses or reduces the distortion of the casting, especially during the unloading of low
pressure die moulds.

Summary

Boron-nitride-coatings have an excellent thermal and chemical stability in the temperature
range that is of interest to aluminium casters. It does not react with the metal melt or the
refractory nor does it disintegrate. Boron nitride shows a very good non-wetting behaviour, one
of the best known in the fields of ceramics. Boron nitride is an excellent high-temperature
lubricant; therefore  it is an excellent lubrication and parting agent when unloading castings
from the moulds or removing remains of aluminium from the casting machines. Boron nitride is
of white colour. Therefore, in contrast to graphite,  it is a good way to keep the casthouse /
foundry cleaner.

## 1. pastukhov2006wettingofgraphite pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000003)

         WETTING OF GRAPHITE SURFACE BY
          THE ALUMINIUM ALLOYS MELTS

                E.A. Pastukhov, V.P. Chentsov, A.V. Kiselev, L.E. Bodrova,
                A.V. Dolmatov, E.A. Popova, S.A. Petrova, R.G. Zacharov

                        Institute of Metallurgy UB RAS Ekaterinburg

       Cast composite materials production (CCM) Al-MeCx by the strengthening phase
synthesis in the aluminium melts demands good wettability of the graphite particles by
matrix melt participating in the carbide strengthening phase formation reactions [1,2].
Other problem in CCM production with an aluminium matrix is active formation an
undesirable Al4C3 phase - which is easily decayed by water with aluminium hydroxide
and methane formation [3].
      Formation of intermediate layer having good bond both with matrix metal and
nonmetallic particle on the interfacial surface may provide reliable wetting of graphite
particles by aluminium melt [3]. The greatest wetting ability of graphite is proper to
carbide formatting transition metals of 4-6 periods, Al, Si, B and some rare earth
elements [4]. Transition metals doping is used to increase wetting of carbon substrates by
metal melts. The elements reducing surface tension of melts and having segregation
tendency on an interfacial surface are also used for this purpose. [2].
      Wetting  angles  temperature dependences  of  graphite  substrates  wetting by
aluminium and its alloys are investigated in the given work. The researches are done to
define optimum temperatures for cast composites production with Al-matrix by carbide
strengthening phase synthesis  in melt.  Possibility of Al4C3 formation  limitation  in
aluminium and its alloys are also investigated.
      Pure aluminium, Al-12%Si and Al-3-3,5%Ti alloys were used for researching of
graphite temperature dependence of wettability. Plane-parallel graphite plates were used
as substrates.
       Experimental installation for wetting angle measuring is described in [5]. The
sample was heated in the horizontal cylindrical chamber in which 10-5 mm mercury
vacuum was achieved. Photos of drop under investigation have been taken by digital
camera, and the images were treated by personal computer.  Wetting angles Θ were
measured by using the images analysis program SIAMS 600 with 0,3-0,60 accuracy.
      During heating in vacuum right after melting the drop of metal has been covered
by oxide coating which stayed up to temperature, approximately, 12000С. Then the
coating has been destroyed and drop was spread on the graphite surface. Therefore the
separate heating system of alloy and graphite substrate for researching of graphite wetting
by liquid aluminium and its alloys at lower temperatures has been constructed. Specimen
has been molten in graphite container and was pressed out on the substrate surface at
given temperature. This technique allows forming a drop without oxide coating already
after heating a substrate to the chosen temperature.
      Wetting angles had been measured in 1000-1300 оС temperature interval by 20 оС
steps staying during 5 minutes at each temperature.
      Wetting angles measurement  results  are shown  at  fig.  1. We  notice slow
decreasing of wetting angles Θfor all alloys in temperature interval 1000-1150 0С. This


                                    1-178decreasing is caused by weak interaction of the molten metal with graphite [3,4]. It’s also
can be seen, that wetting angles for Al and Al-Ti alloy are in good coincidence. Wetting
of  graphite  sharply  increases  with  temperature  growth above  11500С. Chemical
interaction of metal with carbon [3,4] begins  at  this stage. According to data  [3],
aluminium at 1200 0С spreads on graphite up to wetting angle 380 after 13 minutes, then
process stops and there is an intensive formation of aluminium carbides. Adhesion to
graphite in an interval 1100-12000С increases from 0,15 up to 1,52joules/m2 [3]. Wetting
angles of aluminium on graphite decreases to 85o at 1200 0C in our experiments during 5
minutes. Foaming of metal drops (fig. 2 a, b), further began caused probably by increase
of volume at carbide formation process. And the system passed from liquid to the liquid-
solid state.
      Temperature growth above 12000С resulted in the even greater distortion of the
drop form, spreading the liquid aluminium with thin coating formation on the graphite
substrate surface and inflows on the metal drop surface. From the x-ray phase analysis
data the structure of aluminium drop is presented by aluminium carbide Al4C3, two
carbon modifications and one unidentified phase.
      The Al4C3 compound in difference with [6] formed in our experiments is not
accumulated on interfacial boundary, but is regularly distributed in all volume of the
aluminium drop.
      The carbide forming processes are defined by its relative carbide forming ability
after adding Si and Ti elements to aluminium. Standard Gibbs energy of carbide
formation for these elements in recalculation for 1 gram-atom of carbon decreases in
sequence Ti →Al →Si (-164,3; -47,2; -43,1 kilojoules/gram-atom. accordingly) [7].

JOURNAL  OF MATERIALS  SC1ENCE  25 (1990)  2679-2689
Some observations on the wetting and bonding
of nitride ceramics


M.  G. NICHOLAS*,   D.  A. MORTIMER,   L. M. JONES,  R. M. CRISPIN
Materials Development Division, B552 Harwefl Laboratory, United Kingdom Atomic Energy
Authority, Oxfordshire, OXI 10RA


Several series of experiments have been conducted to gain information about the wettability of
AIN, BN, Si3N 4 and two sialon ceramics by potential braze materials.  It was possible to
achieve wetting  of all five ceramics using aluminium, copper-titanium  alloys, and a
Ag-28Cu-2Ti  alloy. Wetting by aluminium and the Ag-28Cu-2Ti  alloy was usually good. Both
wetting and non-wetting  alloys containing titanium reacted to form TiN and  it is argued that
the achievement of wettability  is associated with a certain degree of hypostoichiometry. While
aluminium should also have reacted, no clear evidence was obtained.  In supplementary experi-
ments  it was found that bonds formed by brazing with aluminium  at 1000~  could have shear
strengths as great as 60 MPa. Although the experimental work was preliminary in nature,  it
suggested that good brazing systems could be developed.
